reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive neuroacanthocytosis caused by variants in the XK gene, so affected patients are almost always male with maternally related pedigrees
Loss of the XK protein reduces expression of the Kell blood-group antigens, defining the McLeod red-cell phenotype detectable on blood-group serology
Presents in mid-adult life with chorea, dystonia and a subcortical movement disorder, often with psychiatric and cognitive change resembling other neuroacanthocytoses
Cardiomyopathy and cardiac arrhythmia are important systemic features that may dominate the prognosis
A myopathy with raised creatine kinase and a chronic axonal neuropathy with reduced or absent reflexes are common
Acanthocytes are present on blood film and haemolysis with compensated anaemia may occur
Recognition matters for transfusion safety, as these patients can develop antibodies to Kell antigens and require carefully matched or autologous blood
reference.pathophysiology: McLeod syndrome arises from pathogenic variants in the XK gene on the X chromosome, which encodes a membrane transport-related protein that is covalently linked to the Kell glycoprotein on the red-cell surface. Loss of XK weakens the erythrocyte membrane, producing acanthocytes and the McLeod blood-group phenotype with depressed Kell antigen expression. The same protein is expressed in brain, muscle and heart, and its deficiency drives striatal neurodegeneration, skeletal myopathy, peripheral neuropathy and a dilated cardiomyopathy, giving the characteristic multisystem picture.
additionalDifferentials: Huntington disease and Huntington disease-like disorders
Other causes of dilated cardiomyopathy with neurological features
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film for acanthocytes using incubated wet-film technique
Kell blood-group phenotyping to identify the McLeod red-cell phenotype
Serum creatine kinase and markers of haemolysis
Cardiac assessment with electrocardiography and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia
Brain MRI for caudate atrophy and nerve conduction studies for neuropathy
redFlags: Cardiac symptoms, syncope or arrhythmia suggesting cardiomyopathy that may be fatal
Need for blood transfusion, where mismatched Kell-positive blood risks a severe reaction
New seizures or rapid neurological decline
reference.prognosis: McLeod syndrome is a slowly progressive multisystem disorder; neurological disability accrues over years, but cardiac involvement with cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia is a leading cause of morbidity and premature death, so cardiac surveillance is central to care.
pitfalls: Transfusing standard donor blood without recognising the McLeod phenotype, risking alloimmune reactions
Attributing the movement disorder solely to Huntington disease and missing the X-linked pattern
Failing to screen for cardiomyopathy in a patient labelled as a pure movement disorder
Assuming a normal chorein result excludes neuroacanthocytosis, since McLeod syndrome requires XK and Kell testing
